title: Trustworthy AI Helper - Design & Test the Data (Part 1 Core)
summary: Students design a small AI helper from three parts - a task, a structured prompt and data - then run a clean-versus-noisy data test and explain how data quality changed the output.
objectives: Design a small prompt-driven AI helper: state the task, the structured prompt, and the data it will use.
Test how the quality of the data changes the helper's output, and explain the effect.

body: Over four lessons (two weeks, Core and Lab) you will build a **Trustworthy AI Helper** and prove it can be trusted.
Today you design it and test how the data quality changes its output.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can design a helper with a clear task, a structured prompt, and a data set.
I can test how data quality changes the output and explain why.

terms.definition: A small AI solution that completes a task using a prompt and data.
A precise instruction: goal, details, and the form of the answer.
How accurate, balanced, and complete the data is.

sections.heading: A helper has three parts
body: A [[helper]] is a small solution: a task, a structured prompt, and data.
Its output comes from the data and the prompt, so if the data is poor, the output is poor - even with a good prompt.

sections.heading: Test the data quality
body: Feed your helper clean data, then noisy data, and compare the outputs.
This shows how much the [[data quality]] matters. Poorer data usually gives a poorer, less fair output.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Design your helper, then test clean vs noisy data.
items: Run on clean data; note the output.

worksheet.title: Week 5 - Core - Worksheet | Trustworthy AI Helper - Design & Test the Data (Part 1 Core)

questions.stem:
Task: ...
Structured prompt (goal | details | form): ...
Data: ...
questions.lookFor: All three parts present and clear: a single clear task (e.g. 'recommend one library book'), a structured prompt that names the goal, the details and the form of the answer (e.g. 'Using the class survey, suggest one book most pupils would enjoy, in one sentence with a reason'), and named data (e.g. the balanced reading survey). Accept any clear task + structured prompt + named data. Mastery = clear task, structured prompt and named data; partial = two of three, or one unclear.
questions.prompt: Write the task, a structured prompt, and the data.

questions.stem:
Clean-data output: ...
Noisy-data output: ...
The difference is because ...
questions.lookFor: A genuine clean-vs-noisy comparison with a stated data-quality-to-output effect, e.g. 'on clean data it suggested a popular adventure book; on noisy data (a duplicated entry) it over-suggested one title - poorer data gave a less fair output'. Look for the causal link back to the data, not just two different outputs. Watch for the misconception that a good prompt fixes bad data.
questions.prompt: Record the output on clean data and on noisy data, and explain the difference.

questions.stem: Columns: Helper part | My design | Data-quality finding
questions.lookFor: A completed log covering each helper part (task, structured prompt, data) with a matching data-quality finding. This is the evidence for the formative check: designs a helper with a clear task, structured prompt and data, and explains how data quality changed the output. Record CU and SD as mastery/partial/not-yet.
questions.prompt: Record your design and your data-quality test.

questions.lookFor: One sentence saying the output is produced from the data and the prompt, so poor data gives a poor output even when the prompt is good - the helper does not 'know' the answer. Reject answers implying a strong prompt can fix bad data.
questions.prompt: Write one sentence: why does your helper need good data as well as a good prompt?

questions.lookFor: A reasoned threshold (a proportion or a number of bad entries) tied to the helper's own data and task, with reasoning about when the pattern the helper relies on would be swamped or skewed - e.g. one duplicated entry in a small survey already tips the recommendation. Reasoning matters more than the number.
questions.prompt: Predict how much noise your data can take before the output becomes untrustworthy, and explain your reasoning.
